reasoning: All 12 edits were kept. Each targets a distinct, existing line outside the protected section, and I checked that every target string matches the current skill text. The failure edits come first and keep their wording: the real-people list replacement, brand and species trimming, franchise epithets, possessive/owner pointers, the bare catchphrase rule, ROLE CHECK, and match-the-clue's-own-form. The success edits add patterns the failure edits do not cover: quoted slogan/lyric clues, translation glosses, pun homophones, all-caps flashcards and multi-clue archive dumps, the hedge-phrase caveat to the options rule, bare definition clues, and former-name clues. The failure catchphrase edit and the success quoted-slogan edit sit close together but do not conflict. The first maps a bare exclamation to the show or character, and the second maps a slogan or quotation to the person or author it belongs to. No direct conflicts needed resolving, so the failure versions stand wherever they overlap.

edits.target: If the list is of real people, answer with the team, state or other entity they share.
edits.content: If the list is of real people (a bare list, or a pair joined by '&' with no 'this'), the answer is the ONE proper-noun entity they all belong to: the country or realm a king, queen, prince or princess ruled or belongs to, or the state, party, team or school the passages tie to all of them. 'Ferdinand VII, Juan Carlos' -> 'Spain'; 'Princess Caroline & Princess Stephanie' -> 'Monaco'; 'Edward Kennedy, John Kerry' -> 'Massachusetts'. NEVER answer with one person from the list (not 'Juan Carlos I', not 'Ted Kennedy'), a relationship or role word ('sisters', 'brothers', 'monarchs'), or a generic group label. Use the passages' repeated 'X of <Place>' / 'Prince of <Place>' phrasing to find the shared place.

The same goes for product-type words after a brand ('Hallmark', not 'Hallmark Cards'; 'Nike', not 'Nike Shoes') and for 'Inc.', 'Corp.', 'Airlines' or 'Records' when the bare brand names the company. For an animal or plant, give the plain common name that fits the clue's own descriptors ('lamprey', not 'sea lamprey', when the clue says 'freshwater'). Do not add a habitat, type or place modifier that comes only from a passage.

edits.target: Modifiers copied from passages (hot air, synthetic, funeral, speech) are usually wrong unless part of the standard proper name.
edits.content: - Franchise/character clues: when the clue gives different epithets for one character in different years or releases ('In '84 he's a destroyer, in '82 he was just a barbarian'), the epithets are the clue's words, not the answer. Answer with the one name common to all of them ('Conan'), not a particular title that contains an epithet ('Conan the Destroyer').

edits.target: asks for the title or category noun itself (Dalai Lama), not the individual named in the clue.
edits.content: - Possessive / owner pointers: when the clue says 'his/her 1882 drama', 'this organization's Hall of Fame', 'this man sued ...', the thing named in the clue (a title, a hall of fame, a lawsuit topic) is only an ANCHOR. The answer is the person or body that owns, wrote, founded or did it. '"En Folkefiende" is the Norwegian title of his 1882 drama' -> 'Henrik Ibsen' (not 'En folkefiende'). 'Nancy Lopez & Beth Daniel are in this organization's Hall of Fame, founded in 1967' -> 'LPGA' (the organization that founded it, not 'World Golf Hall of Fame'). 'In the 1950s this man sued the Topeka Board of Education over which school his daughter might attend' -> 'Oliver Brown' (a person's name, never a description like 'segregated school'). Scan the passages for the person or body that is paired with the clue's details.

edits.target: The context passages about the topic usually reveal the link.
edits.content: - A bare quoted catchphrase or exclamation ('"Yabba Dabba Do!"') with no other context asks for the show, character or person it belongs to ('The Flintstones'). Passage titles that merely contain the quoted words (a TV movie or video called 'I Yabba-Dabba Do!') are search hits, not the answer. Name the franchise or origin they all point back to.

edits.target: Do not choose one that fits only some.
edits.content: - ROLE CHECK for person clues: the descriptors in the clue ('former first lady', 'president of the Senate', 'wife of ...') must hold for the candidate at the time of the event. The most famous or most frequent name in the passages is often a distractor (the sitting president, not the former first lady). Search the passages for the descriptor itself next to the event ('Eight candidates, including former First Lady Imelda Marcos') and answer with that person ('Imelda Marcos'), even if she appears in only one passage.

edits.target: Still apply the person-name rule above.
edits.content: - Match the clue's own form. If the clue already names the person in a particular form ('announced that George Bush won'), answer in that same form ('George Bush'), not the encyclopedic 'George H. W. Bush' with added initials. Conversely, when the clue never states the type word ('The Great Lakes are Huron, Ontario, Michigan, Erie & this one ...'), the standard full name includes it ('Lake Superior', not bare 'Superior'). The delete-clue-words test only strips words the clue actually contains.

edits.target: answer with the common English name (Conch).
edits.content:
- A clue that is only a quoted slogan, motto, lyric, line of verse or famous quotation, with no 'this' pointer ('"Tippecanoe and Tyler too"', '"I think that I shall never see a poem lovely as a tree"'), asks WHO or WHAT it belongs to. Answer with the single person or named thing the passages tie to it: the candidate the slogan promoted ('William Henry Harrison') or the author of the line ('Joyce Kilmer'). Do not answer with the slogan, the campaign, a running mate named inside it, a song, or the poem title, unless the clue says 'this poem/song'. Take the entity that recurs across passage titles and sits next to the quoted line.
- Translation clues ('"Mi Vida Loca" translates to this in English', 'in English, this is...'): the passages print the English gloss in parentheses or beside the foreign title ('Mi Vida Loca (My Crazy Life)'). Copy that gloss without quotation marks. Ignore speaker intros or asides such as '(Hi, I'm Pam Tillis)'.

edits.target: Look for passages where that word appears next to a candidate and answer with that candidate.
edits.content: - Pun clues: a quoted homophone ('a large "steak" in British politics', 'The Marquess of this') points to a compound the passages contain ('Salisbury steak'). Answer with the bare name that pairs with the pun word ('Salisbury'), not the pun word itself, the title ('Marquess of') or the full compound.

edits.target: - Archive lines may also be formatted 'CATEGORY | clue text | answer'. Take the answer that follows the clue, even if the whole context is one short passage.
edits.content:
- Flashcard sites such as StudyStack often print the clue and its answer in one all-caps run, with the answer as the last item after a comma ('...EMOTIONAL IN EFFECT & IMPROVISATIONAL IN NATURE, RHAPSODY'). Treat the final item after the clue as the archived answer and copy it, ignoring the surrounding noisy passages.
- In multi-clue archive dumps (GitHub question files, TriviaBistro pages) several 'clue | answer. right: Name.' entries sit back to back. Locate the entry whose clue text matches the question, then take the answer after THAT clue's '|'. The answer on the line above belongs to a different clue, and the contestant name after 'right:' is not part of the answer. If the snippet cuts off before the answer, answer with the entity the other passages tie to the clue's details.

edits.target: - Clue lists its own options ('Of North Park, East Park, West Park or South Park, it's where...'): the answer is exactly one of the listed options, copied verbatim. Use the context to pick which.
edits.content: - Do NOT apply that rule to a hedge about the category ('Whether it's a fruit or vegetable, it's the basis of pomodoro & marinara sauces', 'whether you call it X or Y'). The listed words are a side-comment, not the answer. Answer the concrete thing the rest of the clue describes ('Tomato'), as a plain common noun.

edits.target: - Double-meaning clues ('Term for an international match, or what its players are "put to"', 'X, or Y'): the answer is ONE word that satisfies BOTH halves ('the Test': a Test match; 'put to the test'). Check every candidate against both halves. A dictionary synonym that fits only one half ('trial') is wrong. When passages are noisy, use your own knowledge of sports terms and idioms.
edits.content:
- Bare definition clues with no 'this' ('A short, witty saying') ask for the word being defined. Find the dictionary or thesaurus line that gives the same gloss ('epigram: a witty, ingenious, or pointed saying tersely expressed') and answer with that headword alone, in singular dictionary form. Ignore crossword-solver pages that only repeat the clue. Do not answer with a longer descriptive phrase or a loose synonym such as 'quip' unless the passages gloss it in the clue's own words.
- Former-name clues ('His name, pre-Muhammad Ali', 'née', 'formerly', 'born as'): the answer is the OTHER name, never the one already in the clue. Choose the short form the passages repeat most ('Cassius Clay', not 'Cassius Marcellus Clay Jr.' and not a transient alias like 'Cassius X').
